catalog_quote: I show that the tonal system of Paicî is best described with three underlying primitives: a High tone, a Low tone, and a downstep /Ť/ analyzed as a register feature independent of tone. ... (iv) it has accentual properties, and very likely derives from a former accentual system. ... phonological downstep appears between two adjacent L-toned feet, as a form of dissimilation: *(LL)(LL) → (LL)Ť(LL). ... Note that there is no effect of the foot or colon on the realization of H tones in all-H words; there is thus evidence for foot and colon structure only in L-toned words. ... Phonological downstep in Paicî shares two of these properties: it is culminative within the prosodic word (cf. sweep_summary: Single works with stress in the title (Lionnet 2019, WCCFL 36) was already held by the project with a native text layer and was read in full; written under It is a prosody paper about tone/downstep and foot-colon structure in Paicî, not about word stress; it never attributes stress or accent to Paicî and confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding (its deciding source, Lionnet 2022 PDA, is the fuller peer-reviewed sequel by the same author and remains the better citation). No new stress statement found; nothing to acquire. Leads seen only as bibliographic records in the 2019/2022 reference lists, not downloaded: Rivierre 1974 'Tons et segments du discours en paicî' (BSL 69:1, 325-340) and Rivierre 1978 'Accents, tons et inversion tonale en Nouvelle-Calédonie' (BSL 73:1) — the latter is the historical-accent source (Xârâcùù initial accent vs. Paicî downstep) that the catalog already summarises via Lionnet 2022 §6.4; medium priority if a first-hand French statement of the pre-tonogenesis accent is ever wanted. web look-ups were unnecessary for the single item.

new_statements.quote: Paicî is a tonal language. The tone-bearing unit is the mora. ... Downstep is illustrated in (6): while L-toned words of one to three morae are realized with a level L tone throughout (6a), words of four morae and above undergo a register drop after the second mora (6b). ... As seen, downstep can only occur if there are two adjacent L-toned bimoraic feet, i.e. if there are at least four morae.
new_statements.citation: Lionnet, Florian. 2019. The colon as a separate prosodic category: tonal evidence from Paicî (Oceanic, New Caledonia). Proceedings of WCCFL 36, 250-259. Cascadilla Proceedings Project.
new_statements.reading: Not a stress statement: the paper's only first-hand word-prosodic claim for Paicî is that it is a two-tone, mora-counting language whose L-toned words of four or more morae get a downstep after the initial bimoraic foot (left-edge foot/colon parsing visible only through tone). No word stress or accent is posited; the author frames the metrical structure as tonal, not stress-based. This is the earlier, shorter version of the same author's 2022 PDA article that the catalog already uses, and it agrees with the catalog's 'tonal' coding.

sources.quote: Paicî is a tonal language. The tone-bearing unit is the mora. Only vowels are moraic in Paicî, where coda consonants are not allowed. ... [§2.2] Downstep is illustrated in (6): while L-toned words of one to three morae are realized with a level L tone throughout (6a), words of four morae and above undergo a register drop after the second mora (6b). ... [§3.1] As seen, downstep can only occur if there are two adjacent L-toned bimoraic feet, i.e. if there are at least four morae.
sources.locator: §2.1 p.252 (tonal inventory); §2.2 pp.252-253 (downstep, ex. 6); §3.1 p.254; §4.1 pp.255-256 (prosodic word = tonal nucleus + enclitics, one downstep per prosodic word); §1 p.251 (metrical structure 'in domains other than stress, e.g. tone')
sources.note: Nothing about word stress in Paicî: the word 'stress' occurs only for other languages (Hungarian, Passamaquoddy, Iquito etc.) and in the framing claim that metrical structure is relevant 'in domains other than stress, e.g. tone'. Paicî is described as a two-tone (H vs L) mora-counting language with a metrically conditioned downstep between the first two L-toned bimoraic feet of a prosodic word of 4+ morae (analysed with a colon grouping two feet), plus a juncture H tone on the initial mora/foot of a complement.
